title: Cooling
alt: A section through a one-storey data hall with two air-cooled chillers on the roof. In-row coolers stand between the racks. Chilled water runs down from the chillers in round blue pipes to every cooler; warm water runs back up in round red pipes. Fans on the chillers throw the heat away into the outside air, drawn as rising red air lines. For the hours when outside air alone can do the cooling, the compressor in each chiller is grey and off, and cold outside air, drawn blue, flows through the chiller coils; on the other hours the compressors are orange and running.
sources: Chilled water supply at least 13 degrees C, return about 18 degrees C for an air-cooled hall: NREL / US DOE FEMP 2024

Hours a year outside air alone can do the cooling at an 18 degrees C rack inlet: about 7,100 in Vancouver and 7,600 in Edmonton; the remaining hours (about 1,650 and 1,150) are when compressors run: computed from Canadian weather files for energy calculations (CWEC 2000-2017), derived
Chiller rating about 1,490 kW at 35 degrees C outside: Vertiv Liebert AFC FIZ135, preliminary maker data
drawn_generically: chillers, fans, coils, compressors, pipes, racks and coolers: generic shapes; two chillers drawn, not the layout's count
the compressor shown simply as on (orange) or off (grey); the real changeover point is not in the register
heat thrown away is drawn as red air, not violet, because it is not reused
the hours are for 18 degrees C air into the servers, from weather files; the point where a real chiller switches its compressors on is not shown and not sourced
camera: the hall and roof, then the roof close up for the season steps, then the whole loop

steps.caption: The data hall below, with in-row coolers between the racks. On the roof, two air-cooled chillers.
The chillers send chilled water down to the coolers. It comes back warm, carrying the heat from the servers.
Fans on top of the chillers throw that heat away into the outside air. None of it is used.
For most hours of the year the outside air alone is cold enough to do the cooling, with the servers taking in air at 18 °C: about 7,100 hours a year in Vancouver and 7,600 in Edmonton.
On the other hours, about 1,650 a year in Vancouver and 1,150 in Edmonton, the compressors run to make the water cold enough.
The whole loop: chilled water down, warm water up, heat out to the air.
